items.q: What is Yellowstone's record low temperature?
items.f: It was recorded in 1933 near the West Entrance. The park's record high is 99°F, set at Mammoth in 2002.

items.q: Besides Old Faithful, rangers predict eruptions for four other geysers. Which is one of them?
items.f: The predicted five are Old Faithful, Castle, Grand, Daisy and Riverside. Check the Old Faithful Visitor Education Center for times.
items.s: National Park Service: Current Geyser Activity

items.q: Kiowa tradition holds that at which Yellowstone hot spring their creator gave them the Yellowstone area?
items.f: Many tribes have deep ties to Yellowstone, and 27 tribes are associated with the park today.
items.s: National Park Service: Dragon's Mouth Spring

items.q: In what year was Yellowstone established as the world's first national park?
items.f: President Ulysses S. Grant signed the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act on March 1, 1872.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: In July 2024, a hydrothermal explosion destroyed a boardwalk in which Yellowstone geyser basin?
items.f: Water beneath Black Diamond Pool suddenly flashed to steam, throwing rocks and debris hundreds of feet into the air. Nobody was hurt.
items.s: U.S. Geological Survey: Biscuit Basin Explosion

items.q: Echinus Geyser at Norris is the world's largest geyser of what kind?
items.f: Its water is about as acidic as vinegar. Acid geysers are very rare, and most of the world's are at Norris.

items.q: Which Yellowstone hotel, designed by Robert Reamer and built in 1903–04, is one of the few log hotels left in the U.S.?
items.f: The inn is a National Historic Landmark. Its lobby ceiling is 65 feet high.

items.q: The NPS calls Yellowstone's Lamar Buffalo Ranch the birthplace of what?
items.f: It was the first effort to save a wild species through intensive management.
items.s: National Park Service: Lamar Buffalo Ranch

items.q: About how old are the fossil forests on Yellowstone's Specimen Ridge?
items.f: Scientists have counted at least 27 layers of fossil trees stacked in the ridge, many still standing upright.
items.s: National Park Service: Fossil Plants of Yellowstone

items.q: Which 1870 expedition gave Old Faithful its name?
items.f: The explorers named the geyser for how regularly it erupted.
items.s: National Park Service: Old Faithful Geyser

items.q: Yellowstone's colorful bubbling mudpots are sometimes called what?
items.f: Minerals in the mud give mudpots so many colors that they earned the nickname 'paint pots.'

items.q: How tall is Yellowstone's Tower Fall?
items.f: The waterfall is named for the tower-like rock spires at its brink.

items.q: About how much snow falls in Yellowstone in an average year?
items.f: Higher elevations can get double that.

items.q: How fast can a bison run?
items.f: Bison can also jump over objects about 5 feet high. Bulls weigh up to about 2,000 pounds.

items.q: The 1959 Hebgen Lake earthquake near Yellowstone killed how many people?
items.f: A huge landslide in Madison Canyon was part of the disaster.
items.s: U.S. Geological Survey: Hebgen Lake Earthquake

items.q: Yellowstone stretches into three states. Which of these is NOT one of them?
items.f: About 96% of the park is in Wyoming, 3% in Montana and 1% in Idaho.

items.q: Which Yellowstone peak has a fire lookout staffed all summer that hikers can visit?
items.f: A lookout lives at the 10,219-foot summit from mid-June until fire season ends, watching for smoke.

items.q: In 1959, a magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck just west of Yellowstone near which lake?
items.f: By the next day, at least 289 springs in the Firehole River basins had erupted as geysers, and 160 of them had no record of ever erupting before.

items.q: Which feature of Yellowstone's Old Faithful Visitor Education Center helps protect the land around it?
items.f: It's also where you can check the next predicted eruption times.
items.s: National Park Service: Old Faithful Visitor Education Center

items.q: Which Yellowstone grizzlies usually leave their winter dens first?
w: They all wake up the same day
items.f: Males often come out in early March, and mothers with cubs follow in April and May.
items.s: National Park Service: First Grizzly Sighting of 2026

items.q: Which animal lives in Yellowstone today but is NOT native to the Greater Yellowstone area?
items.f: They descend from goats released in Montana mountain ranges in the 1940s and 1950s, and they reached the park in the 1990s.

items.q: Excelsior Geyser Crater pours more than how much hot water per minute into the Firehole River?
items.f: Excelsior once erupted more than 300 feet high in the late 1800s. Today it acts as a giant hot spring.
items.s: National Park Service: Excelsior Geyser Crater

items.q: Which Yellowstone entrance is open to regular cars all year?
items.f: The only road usually open to regular vehicles all year runs from the North Entrance at Gardiner, Montana, through Tower Junction to Cooke City.

items.q: About how many mammal species live in Yellowstone?
items.f: They include two kinds of bears and seven native hoofed mammals.

items.q: How many entrances does Yellowstone have?
items.f: The park has 392 miles of paved roads and more than 15 miles of boardwalk.

items.q: Why has Morning Glory Pool lost much of its deep blue color?
items.a: Visitors threw coins and trash in
items.f: The junk clogged the vent and the water cooled, so orange and yellow bacteria spread toward the center of the pool.
items.s: National Park Service: Morning Glory Pool

items.q: Which pass is the trailhead for the popular hike up Mount Washburn?
items.f: The trailhead parking lot is 4.5 miles north of Canyon Junction.
items.s: National Park Service: Dunraven Pass–Mount Washburn Trail

items.q: Which group took charge of Yellowstone in 1886?
items.f: The Army arrived on August 20, 1886, and later built Fort Yellowstone at Mammoth. Many of its red-roofed buildings are still in use.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: What is the largest wild waterfowl in North America, found in Yellowstone?
items.f: Their wingspan can reach 8 feet. Around 1930, a small group in the Greater Yellowstone area helped the species survive.

items.q: About how many hydrothermal features does Yellowstone have?
items.f: That count includes more than 500 active geysers, which is over half of all the geysers in the world.

items.q: Whose photographs, along with Thomas Moran's paintings, helped convince Congress to protect Yellowstone?
items.f: Jackson's photographs and Moran's paintings showed lawmakers back East what the West really looked like.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: Which is Yellowstone's hottest thermal area?
items.f: A scientific drill hole at Norris recorded 459°F just 1,087 feet below the surface, the highest temperature measured in any Yellowstone thermal area.
items.s: National Park Service: Norris Geyser Basin

items.q: A microbe discovered in a Yellowstone hot spring made which scientific tool possible?
items.f: Thomas Brock and Hudson Freeze described Thermus aquaticus in 1969. Its heat-resistant enzyme, Taq polymerase, makes PCR work.
items.s: National Park Service: Discovering Life in Yellowstone

items.q: In 1872, Congress paid $10,000 for Thomas Moran's huge painting of what?
items.a: The Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone
items.f: The 7-by-12-foot canvas was bought just months after Yellowstone became a park and hung in the U.S. Capitol.

items.q: Which animal is the most numerous large mammal in Yellowstone?
items.f: In summer, 10,000 to 20,000 elk live in the park. Fewer than 2,000 stay through the winter.

items.q: About how often does Grand Geyser erupt?
items.f: Each eruption lasts 9 to 12 minutes, so rangers post predictions to help visitors catch it.
items.s: National Park Service: Grand Geyser Stop

items.q: Why can't you soak in Yellowstone's Boiling River right now?
items.a: It has been closed since the 2022 floods
w: It dried up in an earthquake
items.f: The 2022 flood was called a 500-year event and changed the Gardner River where the Boiling River meets it.
items.s: National Park Service: Swimming in Yellowstone

items.q: Which Yellowstone geyser shoots at an angle across the Firehole River?
items.f: Riverside is in the Upper Geyser Basin, not far from Old Faithful.

items.q: About how many bison lived in Yellowstone before calving season in 2025?
items.f: In 1901, only about 25 were counted, so the herd's comeback is a conservation success story.

items.q: What is the largest hot spring in Yellowstone?
items.f: Grand Prismatic is 200 to 330 feet across and more than 121 feet deep. Its rainbow rings come from heat-loving microbes called thermophiles.
items.s: National Park Service: Grand Prismatic Spring

items.q: Which Yellowstone geyser is the tallest predictable geyser in the world?
items.f: Grand erupts in powerful bursts up to about 200 feet. Steamboat goes higher, but nobody can predict when.

items.q: In late summer, grizzlies climb to high rocky slopes near Yellowstone to eat thousands of what?
items.f: Army cutworm moths hide under rocks, and they're one of the richest foods a grizzly can find.
items.s: National Park Service: Bear Food Habits

items.q: What is the highest point in Yellowstone National Park?
items.f: Eagle Peak reaches 11,358 feet. The park's lowest point is Reese Creek, at 5,282 feet.

items.q: West Thumb's Fishing Cone got its name because early visitors did what there?
w: Caught fish in its hot water
Used it as a fish hatchery
Spotted fossils of fish in it
items.f: People caught trout in the lake and cooked them in the boiling spring while they were still on the hook. It's banned now because it damaged the cone.

items.q: What gives the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone its yellow walls?
items.a: Iron in rock altered by hot water
items.f: Hot water altered the rhyolite rock, and the iron in it oxidized. The NPS says most of the yellows come from iron and sulfur in the rock.
items.s: National Park Service: Canyon Village and the Grand Canyon

items.q: Harry Yount, hired in Yellowstone in 1880, is often called the first what?
items.f: He was hired as a gamekeeper and spent the winter alone in a cabin, then recommended a paid force of rangers.

items.q: How fast can Yellowstone's pronghorn sprint?
items.f: That speed may be left over from a time when pronghorn had to outrun an American cheetah, which is now extinct.

items.q: About how many visits did Yellowstone get in 2024?
items.f: The 2024 total was 44% higher than in 2022, when historic floods cut off access to parts of the park.

items.q: How do most visitors reach Old Faithful in winter?
items.a: On a guided snowcoach or snowmobile
items.f: The oversnow season usually starts December 15. The only road open to regular cars all winter runs from Gardiner to Cooke City.

items.q: The Yellowstone River is the longest what in the lower 48 states?
items.f: The river flows about 671 miles from the Absaroka Mountains to the Missouri River near the North Dakota line.

items.q: Who led the cavalry that took charge of Yellowstone in 1886?
items.f: He arrived with 50 men, fought fires and set the first strict rules to protect the park.
items.s: National Park Service: Captain Moses Harris

items.q: Yellowstone's Hayden Valley was once covered by what?
items.f: Lake sediments hold water near the surface, which keeps the valley marshy and full of grass for bison.

items.q: In fall, what loud call do bull elk make during mating season?
items.f: The rut runs from early September to mid-October. Bulls are aggressive then, so keep your distance.

items.q: Yellowstone's Gibbon Falls tumbles over the remains of what?
items.a: The rim of the Yellowstone Caldera
items.f: The falls drop 84 feet. The rock wall across the road is part of the caldera's inner rim.

items.q: Yellowstone Lake is North America's largest freshwater lake above what elevation?
items.f: The lake sits at 7,733 feet. It has 141 miles of shoreline and is up to 430 feet deep.

items.q: Which is the oldest hotel still operating in Yellowstone?
items.f: It opened in 1891. Robert Reamer later added its signature columns and false balconies.
items.s: National Park Service: Lake Hotel and Cabins

items.q: How much did Congress set aside for the 1871 Hayden survey of Yellowstone?
items.f: The survey's report, photos and paintings helped convince Congress to create the park in 1872.
items.s: National Park Service: National Parks, The American Experience

items.q: How did the cutthroat trout get its name?
items.a: From a red slash under its jaw
items.f: Yellowstone's native cutthroat also have dark spots, mostly toward the tail.
items.s: National Park Service: Yellowstone Trout Facts

items.q: Most of the water at Yellowstone's Norris Geyser Basin is what?
items.f: Norris is home to rare acid geysers and is the park's hottest thermal area.
items.s: National Park Service: Norris Geyser Basin

items.q: Which bird plants whitebark pine forests by burying the seeds, a food grizzlies also love?
items.f: The bird carries seeds in a pouch under its tongue and buries them, sometimes miles away.

items.q: How tall is the Lower Falls of the Yellowstone River?
items.f: Yellowstone has about 290 waterfalls, and the Lower Falls is the tallest one near a road.

items.q: The green and orange mats around Yellowstone's hot springs are mostly made of what?
items.f: Some of these cyanobacteria grow in water as hot as about 167°F. Their colors change as the water cools.

items.q: Mystic Falls, near Biscuit Basin, drops about how far?
items.f: It's on the Little Firehole River, a short hike from the Old Faithful area.
items.s: National Park Service: Mystic Falls Trail

items.q: When grizzlies were listed as threatened in 1975, about how many lived in the Greater Yellowstone area?
items.f: By 2024 the population was estimated at about 1,030 bears.
items.s: National Park Service: Forty Years of Grizzly Recovery

items.q: The West Thumb of Yellowstone Lake is a caldera inside what?
items.f: An eruption about 174,000 years ago created West Thumb, which is about the same size as Oregon's Crater Lake.
items.s: National Park Service: West Thumb and the South

items.q: Obsidian from Yellowstone's Obsidian Cliff has been found as far away as which region?
items.f: It's the source of about 90% of the obsidian found at Hopewell mound sites in the Ohio River Valley.

items.q: How thick can the ice on Yellowstone Lake get in winter?
items.f: The lake usually freezes in late December or early January and thaws in late May or early June.

items.q: How many kinds of bears live in Yellowstone?
w: Three: grizzly, black and polar bears
items.f: Yellowstone has 67 kinds of mammals, including both bear species.

items.q: Rangers predict Old Faithful's next eruption mostly by measuring what?
items.a: How long the last eruption lasted
items.f: Longer eruptions are followed by longer waits until the next one.
items.s: National Park Service: Old Faithful Virtual Visitor Center

items.q: After waking up in 2018, Steamboat Geyser hit a record of how many eruptions in a single year?
items.f: It erupted 48 times in both 2019 and 2020, after barely erupting for years.

items.q: Which is the world's tallest active geyser?
items.f: Steamboat's major eruptions shoot water more than 300 feet high. It's in the Norris Geyser Basin.

items.q: Which tree makes up most of Yellowstone's forests?
items.f: More than 80% of the park's forest is lodgepole pine.

items.q: French traders gave the Yellowstone River what name?
items.f: The Hidatsa named the river for the yellow sandstone bluffs along it in eastern Montana. French traders translated that name as 'Roche Jaune,' which means 'yellow rock.'

items.q: The terraces at Mammoth Hot Springs are made of what?
items.f: The travertine terraces are always changing, sometimes within a single day.
items.s: National Park Service: Mammoth Hot Springs and the North

items.q: About how often does Yellowstone's Lone Star Geyser erupt?
items.f: It shoots 30 to 45 feet high from a 12-foot cone, at the end of a flat trail you can walk or bike.
items.s: National Park Service: Lone Star Geyser Trail

items.q: About how much of Yellowstone is covered by forest?
items.f: More than 80% of that forest is lodgepole pine.

items.q: Which animal became the official U.S. national mammal in 2016?
items.f: President Obama signed the National Bison Legacy Act on May 9, 2016.
items.s: National Park Service: America's New National Mammal

items.q: Roughly how often does Old Faithful erupt these days?
items.f: As of January 2025, the median wait between eruptions was 102 minutes (give or take 10). Intervals ranged from 54 to 118 minutes.

items.q: Roughly when did the eruption that formed today's Yellowstone Caldera happen?
items.f: The Lava Creek eruption threw out more than 1,000 cubic kilometers of material and left a caldera about 30 by 45 miles.

items.q: Isa Lake, on the Continental Divide at Craig Pass, was once probably the only lake on Earth to drain naturally into what?
items.f: The NPS says this may now happen only at peak snowmelt after winters with deep snow.

items.q: Yellowstone's geysers and hot springs are powered by heat from what?
items.f: Yellowstone sits on one of the world's largest volcanic calderas.

items.q: Which Yellowstone animal declined sharply after the 1988 fires burned its winter forests?
items.f: Unlike moose in many places, Yellowstone's moose rely on old fir forests to survive winter.

items.q: Yellowstone is larger than which two states combined?
items.f: The park covers 3,472 square miles, or about 2.2 million acres.

items.q: Biscuit Basin was named for biscuit-shaped mineral formations around which pool?
items.f: After the 1959 earthquake, Sapphire Pool erupted and blew most of the biscuits away.

items.q: Which Yellowstone hydrothermal features can reach temperatures as high as 280°F?
items.f: The NPS says steam vents are often superheated, reaching temperatures as high as 280°F.

items.q: Which Yellowstone hot spring belches steam out of a cave like a dragon breathing smoke?
items.f: It's next to Mud Volcano, just north of Yellowstone Lake. Earlier names included 'The Belcher.'
items.s: National Park Service: Dragon's Mouth Spring

items.q: Which area has the most geysers in Yellowstone?
items.f: At least 150 hydrothermal features are packed into about one square mile around Old Faithful.

items.q: What has Yellowstone used on Sylvan Pass in winter to set off avalanches safely?
items.f: Controlled avalanches help keep the East Entrance road safe for winter travelers.
items.s: National Park Service: Yellowstone Superintendent's Compendium

items.q: Nearly all of Yellowstone's beaver colonies are found near which plant?
items.f: Willow grows back quickly after beavers cut it. The park estimated 121 beaver colonies in 2024.

items.q: Most of Yellowstone National Park is in which state?
items.f: About 96% of the park is in Wyoming. The rest is in Montana (3%) and Idaho (1%).

items.q: People have been quarrying Yellowstone's Obsidian Cliff for toolmaking for more than how long?
items.f: Obsidian Cliff became a National Historic Landmark in 1996.

items.q: Which president signed the law creating Yellowstone National Park?
items.f: Grant signed the act on March 1, 1872, only six months after the Hayden Expedition explored the area.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: What words are carved on the Roosevelt Arch at the North Entrance?
items.a: For the benefit and enjoyment of the people
items.f: President Theodore Roosevelt placed the arch's cornerstone in 1903, and you can still drive through it all year.
items.s: National Park Service: Mammoth Hot Springs and the North

items.q: About how tall is Yellowstone's Fairy Falls?
items.f: The trail to Fairy Falls also leads to the overlook with the famous view down onto Grand Prismatic Spring.
items.s: National Park Service: Fairy Falls Trail

items.q: Which Yellowstone valley is the world's top spot for watching wild wolves?
items.f: Wolves have been watched there since they returned in 1995. Early morning and evening are best.
items.s: National Park Service: A Peak Experience Watching Wolves

items.q: In what year were gray wolves brought back to Yellowstone?
items.f: The park's last wolf pack was killed in 1926. In 1995 and 1996, 31 gray wolves from western Canada were moved to Yellowstone.
items.s: National Park Service: History of Wolf Management

items.q: About how long is the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone?
items.f: It runs from the Upper Falls to the Tower Fall area and is 800 to 1,200 feet deep.
items.s: National Park Service: Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone

items.q: Yellowstone's West Thumb is about the same size as which famous lake?
items.f: Both fill calderas left by volcanic eruptions.
items.s: National Park Service: West Thumb and the South

items.q: What makes many lodgepole pine cones open up and release their seeds?
items.f: These cones are sealed shut with resin that melts at about 113°F, so a burned forest quickly reseeds itself.
items.s: National Park Service: Ecological Consequences of Fire

items.q: In 1901, about how many bison were counted in Yellowstone?
items.f: Congress then paid to buy 21 bison from private owners, and they were raised in the Lamar Valley to rebuild the herd.
items.s: National Park Service: Lamar Buffalo Ranch

items.q: The NPS says the travertine terraces at Mammoth Hot Springs look like what?
items.f: Hot water rising through limestone builds the terraces, and they can change shape surprisingly fast.

items.q: About what share of the world's active geysers are in Yellowstone?
items.f: Yellowstone has more than 500 active geysers.

items.q: How many Native American tribes have historic ties to Yellowstone?
items.f: Yellowstone also has more than 1,800 known archeological sites.

items.q: How did Old Faithful get its name?
items.a: It erupts on a regular schedule
w: It's the oldest geyser on Earth
A ranger named Faith found it
items.f: An 1870 expedition named it after watching how dependably it erupted.
items.s: National Park Service: Old Faithful Geyser

items.q: Yellowstone's Black Sand Basin is named for sand made from what?
items.f: The basin, about a mile from Old Faithful, has some of the park's most colorful hot springs.
items.s: National Park Service: Black Sand Basin

items.q: About how many earthquakes does Yellowstone have each year?
items.f: Yellowstone sits on an active volcano and has one of the world's largest calderas, about 45 by 30 miles.

items.q: Which non-native fish threatens native cutthroat trout in Yellowstone Lake?
items.f: Gillnetting is the park's main tool for reducing the lake trout population. Crews set the nets in deep water to avoid catching cutthroat.

items.q: In 1896, Black soldiers of the 25th Infantry rode to Yellowstone from Fort Missoula on what?
items.f: The Buffalo Soldier bicycle corps tested whether bikes could replace horses for the Army.
items.s: National Park Service: 25th Infantry Bicycle Corps

items.q: Which gateway town sits at Yellowstone's North Entrance?
items.f: The North Entrance is marked by the Roosevelt Arch, and Gardiner is also home to the park's Heritage and Research Center.
items.s: National Park Service: Mammoth Hot Springs and the North

items.q: Yellowstone's Roosevelt Lodge, finished in 1920, is built from what?
items.f: Theodore Roosevelt camped nearby in 1903, though not at the lodge site itself.

items.q: Which Upper Geyser Basin geyser has a cone thousands of years old and may be the oldest there?
items.f: Its cone and the platform beneath it form one of the largest geyser deposits in the world.

items.q: In 1948, which Yellowstone mudpot exploded into the forest, blowing trees out by their roots?
items.f: It covered the surrounding forest in mud and is still churning beside the Mud Volcano trail.
items.s: National Park Service: Mud Volcano Trail

items.q: Yellowstone's Petrified Tree, near Tower Junction, is an ancient what?
items.f: Redwoods once grew here in a much warmer climate before volcanic mudflows buried them.

items.q: Which clever Yellowstone bird has learned to unzip backpacks to steal food?
items.f: Ravens have figured out many zippers and buckles, so never leave a pack with food unattended.

items.q: Who was Yellowstone's first superintendent?
items.f: Langford took the job even though it came with no pay.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: In 1877, which people crossed Yellowstone in 13 days while fleeing the U.S. Army?
items.f: About 800 men, women and children, with almost 2,000 horses, entered the park on August 23, 1877.
items.s: National Park Service: Flight of the Nez Perce

items.q: Why does Yellowstone's Emerald Pool look green?
items.a: Yellow microbes mixed with blue water
items.f: Microbes create many of Yellowstone's colors. As pools cool, they can turn orange and murky.

items.q: Before Steamboat Geyser woke up in March 2018, how long had it been quiet?
items.f: Its new active phase set records for eruptions per year.
items.s: U.S. Geological Survey: Steamboat Geyser's 2018 Reawakening

items.q: How did Yellowstone's Electric Peak get its name?
items.a: Climbers got caught in a lightning storm near its top
w: It has a power line on top
items.f: Henry Gannett of the 1872 Hayden Survey was so shaken by the storm that he named the 10,969-foot peak for it.

items.q: Why is fishing banned at Fishing Bridge?
items.f: Overfishing had helped cause the trout's decline, so the bridge closed to fishing in 1973. Now it's a good place to watch trout instead.

items.q: Which Yellowstone lake is thought to be the largest lake in the lower 48 states that you can't reach by road?
items.f: Paddlers reach it from Lewis Lake. Motorboats aren't allowed on it.

items.q: How close can you legally get to bears and wolves in Yellowstone?
items.f: Stay at least 25 yards from all other animals, including bison and elk.

items.q: Because of their orange-red color, baby bison are nicknamed what?
items.f: Calves are born in spring and turn dark brown after a few months, when their humps start to grow.
items.s: National Park Service: 15 Facts About Bison

items.q: About how much of Yellowstone burned in the fires of 1988?
items.f: In total, 793,880 acres of the park burned that summer.

items.q: Mammoth's 37-foot Liberty Cap, a dormant hot spring cone, was named after what?
items.a: Caps worn during the French Revolution
items.f: The Hayden Survey named it in 1871. Hot water pushed up through the same opening for a very long time, slowly building the cone.
